claim: In animals, microtubules and centrosomes direct the migration of gamete pronuclei for fertilization.
source: In animals, microtubules and centrosomes direct the migration of gamete pronuclei for fertilization.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about animal fertilization mechanisms, supported by the citation to Schatten, 1994 and Reinsch and Gonczy, 1998 in the Introduction.

claim: Flowering plants have lost essential components of the centrosome.
source: By contrast, flowering plants have lost essential components of the centrosome, raising the question of how flowering plants control gamete nuclei migration during fertilization.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carvalho-Santos et al., 2011 in the Introduction section.

claim: F-actin structures assist the male nucleus during its migration towards the female nucleus in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Live imaging shows that F-actin structures assist the male nucleus during its migration towards the female nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data presented in Figures 2 and 3 and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: A female gamete-specific Rho-GTPase regulates F-actin dynamics in Arabidopsis.
source: We identify a female gamete-specific Rho-GTPase that regulates F-actin dynamics and further show that actin–myosin interactions are also involved in male gamete nucleus migration.
evidence: This is supported by data showing ROP8 expression in central cells (Figure 5) and F-actin dynamics defects in DN-ROP8 lines (Figure 6).

claim: Actin-myosin interactions are involved in male gamete nucleus migration in Arabidopsis.
source: We identify a female gamete-specific Rho-GTPase that regulates F-actin dynamics and further show that actin–myosin interactions are also involved in male gamete nucleus migration.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced F-actin movement in the presence of myosin inhibitors BDM and NEM (Figure 6).

claim: Microtubules are dispensable for migration and fusion of male and female gamete nuclei in Arabidopsis.
source: Genetic analyses and imaging indicate that microtubules are dispensable for migration and fusion of male and female gamete nuclei.
evidence: This is supported by data from por mutants showing successful fertilization despite defective microtubule assembly (Figure 7).

claim: The innovation of a novel actin-based mechanism of fertilization during plant evolution might account for the complete loss of the centrosome in flowering plants.
source: The innovation of a novel actin-based mechanism of fertilization during plant evolution might account for the complete loss of the centrosome in flowering plants.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings and evolutionary context.

claim: Flowering plants have evolved a double fertilization process that requires the fusion of two sperm cells with the two female gametes, the egg cell and the central cell.
source: Flowering plants have evolved a double fertilization process that requires the fusion of two sperm cells with the two female gametes, the egg cell and the central cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about flowering plant reproduction, supported by citation to Kawashima and Berger, 2011.

claim: Sperm cells are immotile and delivered to the female gametes by the pollen tube.
source: Sperm cells are immotile and delivered to the female gametes by the pollen tube.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant reproduction.

claim: Several factors and molecular mechanisms controlling pollen tube guidance and reception have been recently characterized.
source: Several factors and molecular mechanisms controlling these early events such as pollen tube guidance and reception have been recently characterized (Higashiyama et al., 2001; Palanivelu et al., 2003; Kasahara et al., 2005; Escobar-Restrepo et al., 2007; Okuda et al., 2009; Kessler et al., 2010; Tsukamoto et al., 2010; Takeuchi and Higashiyama, 2012; Leydon et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2013; Ngo et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Mechanisms governing plasmogamy have been identified.
source: mechanisms governing plasmogamy have been identified (Mori et al., 2006; Von Besser et al., 2006; Mori et al., 2014; Sprunck et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: How gamete nuclei migrate and fuse in flowering plants still remain largely elusive.
source: However, how gamete nuclei migrate and fuse in flowering plants still remain largely elusive.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: In most animals, microtubules organized by the centrosome control female pronucleus migration towards the male pronucleus.
source: In most animals, microtubules organized by the centrosome control female pronucleus migration towards the male pronucleus (Schatten, 1994; Reinsch and Gonczy, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about animal fertilization, supported by citations.

claim: The essential components of the centrosome have been lost before the emergence of flowering plants.
source: By contrast, the essential components of the centrosome have been lost before the emergence of flowering plants (Carvalho-Santos et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carvalho-Santos et al., 2011.

claim: The sperm cell nucleus moves towards the female gamete nucleus without the participation of centrosomes in flowering plants.
source: the sperm cell nucleus moves towards the female gamete nucleus without the participation of centrosomes in flowering plants.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of centrosome components in flowering plants.

claim: During plant evolution, the basal plants developed actin-based organelle movements.
source: During plant evolution, the basal plants developed actin-based organelle movements (Madison and Nebenfuhr, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Madison and Nebenfuhr, 2013.

claim: Actin-based organelle movements coincided with the centrosome loss in somatic cells in the basal land plants.
source: which coincided with the centrosome loss in somatic cells in the basal land plants (Vaughn and Harper, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vaughn and Harper, 1998.

claim: The genomes of bryophytes, ferns, and most likely certain gymnosperms encode components of the centrosome.
source: However, the genomes of bryophytes, ferns, and most likely certain gymnosperms encode components of the centrosome and these organisms produce a centrosome specifically in spermatogenous cells (Vaughn and Harper, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vaughn and Harper, 1998.

claim: Bryophytes, ferns, and most likely certain gymnosperms produce a centrosome specifically in spermatogenous cells.
source: However, the genomes of bryophytes, ferns, and most likely certain gymnosperms encode components of the centrosome and these organisms produce a centrosome specifically in spermatogenous cells (Vaughn and Harper, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vaughn and Harper, 1998.

claim: Microtubules are essential for gamete nuclear migration in the fern Marsilea vestita.
source: Indeed, microtubules are essential for gamete nuclear migration in the fern Marsilea vestita (Kuligowski et al., 1985)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuligowski et al., 1985.

claim: Gamete nuclear migration without the centrosome in flowering plants evolved separately from the actin-based organelle movement mechanism in somatic cells.
source: these observations imply that gamete nuclear migration without the centrosome in flowering plants evolved separately from the actin-based organelle movement mechanism in somatic cells
evidence: This is an inference based on the evolutionary observations described.

claim: Corona structures of actin filaments around the sperm cells appear at the time of sperm cell release from the pollen tube prior to plasmogamy in many flowering plants.
source: Immunofluorescence approaches revealed that corona structures of actin filaments around the sperm cells appear at the time of sperm cell release from the pollen tube prior to plasmogamy in many flowering plants (Huang and Russell, 1994; Huang and Sheridan, 1998; Huang et al., 1999; Fu et al., 2000; Ye et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous immunofluorescence studies.

claim: Changes in F-actin organization in the egg cell during fertilization are evident.
source: Changes in F-actin organization in the egg cell during fertilization are also evident (Huang et al., 1999; Fu et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An involvement of F-actin in gamete nuclear migration has been suggested during in vitro fertilization in rice.
source: indeed, an involvement of F-actin in gamete nuclear migration has been suggested during in vitro fertilization in rice (Ohnishi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ohnishi et al., 2014.

claim: Lifeact-Venus marks actin cables in the egg cell.
source: To investigate the requirement and function of F-actin during fertilization, we expressed the fluorescent reporter Lifeact-Venus (Riedl et al., 2008; Era et al., 2009) under the control of the egg cell-specific EC1 promoter (Sprunck et al., 2012) to visualize the actin cytoskeleton in the egg cell (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the imaging data in Figure 1B showing fluorescent cables.

claim: Lifeact-Venus marked cables are disassembled after treatment with Latrunculin A.
source: Lifeact-Venus marked cables were disassembled after treatment with the actin polymerizing inhibitor Latrunculin A (LatA; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the imaging data in Figure 1C showing loss of cable structures after LatA treatment.

claim: DN-ACTIN contains one amino acid substitution in the hydrophobic loop of Arabidopsis ACT8.
source: DN-ACTIN contains one amino acid substitution in the hydrophobic loop of Arabidopsis ACT8, which causes instability and fragmentation of actin filaments, leading to incomplete yet strong disruption of actin cytoskeleton (Kato et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kato et al., 2010.

claim: DN-ACTIN causes instability and fragmentation of actin filaments.
source: DN-ACTIN contains one amino acid substitution in the hydrophobic loop of Arabidopsis ACT8, which causes instability and fragmentation of actin filaments, leading to incomplete yet strong disruption of actin cytoskeleton (Kato et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kato et al., 2010 and demonstrated in Figure 1D.

claim: In wild-type plants, fertilization leads to karyogamy followed by decondensation of the chromatin from the male nucleus.
source: In WT plants, fertilization leads to karyogamy followed by decondensation of the chromatin from the male nucleus (Figure 1E; Ingouff et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1E and supported by citation to Ingouff et al., 2007.

claim: Egg cell fertilization initiates embryo development.
source: Egg cell fertilization initiates embryo development while the fusion of the other sperm cell with the central cell leads to endosperm development (Figure 1A,F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant reproduction and demonstrated in Figure 1F.

claim: Fusion of the sperm cell with the central cell leads to endosperm development.
source: Egg cell fertilization initiates embryo development while the fusion of the other sperm cell with the central cell leads to endosperm development (Figure 1A,F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant reproduction and demonstrated in Figure 1F.

claim: Fertilization of the egg cell expressing DN-ACTIN failed as the sperm nucleus did not fuse with the egg cell nucleus and the sperm chromatin remained condensed.
source: By contrast, fertilization of the egg cell expressing DN-ACTIN failed as the sperm nucleus did not fuse with the egg cell nucleus and the sperm chromatin remained condensed (Figure 1G; Line 1, 35% defects in DN-ACTIN [n = 104] compared to 0% defects in WT [n = 98]).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging and quantitative data showing fertilization defects in DN-ACTIN expressing egg cells.

claim: 35% of DN-ACTIN expressing egg cells (Line 1) showed fertilization defects compared to 0% in wild-type.
source: By contrast, fertilization of the egg cell expressing DN-ACTIN failed as the sperm nucleus did not fuse with the egg cell nucleus and the sperm chromatin remained condensed (Figure 1G; Line 1, 35% defects in DN-ACTIN [n = 104] compared to 0% defects in WT [n = 98]).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the experiment.

claim: Karyogamy was prevented only in the egg cell expressing DN-ACTIN but not in the central cell, resulting in a seed containing endosperm without an embryo.
source: Karyogamy was prevented only in the egg cell expressing DN-ACTIN but not in the central cell, resulting in a seed containing endosperm without an embryo [Figure 1H; Line 1, 27% defects in DN-ACTIN (n = 110) compared to 0% defects in WT (n = 389)].
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging and quantitative data showing selective fertilization defects in DN-ACTIN expressing egg cells.

claim: 27% of DN-ACTIN expressing plants (Line 1) showed seed developmental defects compared to 0% in wild-type.
source: Karyogamy was prevented only in the egg cell expressing DN-ACTIN but not in the central cell, resulting in a seed containing endosperm without an embryo [Figure 1H; Line 1, 27% defects in DN-ACTIN (n = 110) compared to 0% defects in WT (n = 389)].
evidence: This is quantitative data from the experiment.

claim: Actin cytoskeletons are required for egg cell fertilization.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that actin cytoskeletons are required for egg cell fertilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the DN-ACTIN and LatA treatment experiments showing fertilization defects.

claim: Other independent transgenic lines expressing DN-ACTIN showed similar seed developmental arrest (Line 2, 20% defects; Line 3, 22% defects).
source: Consistently, other independent transgenic lines showed similar seed developmental arrest [Line 2, 20% defects (n = 125); Line 3, 22% defects (n = 114)].
evidence: This is quantitative data from additional independent transgenic lines.

claim: The central cell is about five times larger than the egg cell.
source: We further investigated the requirement of F-actin during fertilization in the central cell that is about five times larger than the egg cell, thus enabling more detailed F-actin dynamics visualization.
evidence: This is a factual observation about cell size.

claim: F-actin in the wild-type mature central cell is organized in three major distinct structures: a ring-shaped actin network at the micropylar end, long actin cables at the periphery, and a track formed of a bundle of actin cables running from the micropylar actin ring to the central cell nucleus.
source: F-actin in the WT mature central cell showed that F-actin is organized in three major distinct structures: (i) a ring-shaped actin network at the micropylar end of the central cell surrounding the synergid cells and the egg cell; (ii) long actin cables at the periphery of the central cell, extending from the chalazal region to the boundary with the egg cell; and (iii) a track formed of a bundle of actin cables, running from the micropylar actin ring to the central cell nucleus (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The F-actin structures in the central cell disassemble in response to LatA treatment.
source: As expected, these structures disassembled in response to LatA treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: During fertilization, the track of actin cables becomes associated with the migrating sperm cell nucleus in the central cell.
source: During fertilization, the track of actin cables became associated with the migrating sperm cell nucleus in the central cell from the site of fusion between the sperm cell and the central cell to the central cell nucleus (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Time-lapse image analysis confirmed F-actin association to the sperm cell nucleus during its migration in the central cell.
source: Time-lapse image analysis further confirmed F-actin association to the sperm cell nucleus during its migration in the central cell (Figure 3; Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 3 and Video 1.

claim: Upon completion of karyogamy, the micropylar actin ring and bundles of F-actin associated with the sperm cell nucleus disassemble.
source: Upon completion of karyogamy, the micropylar actin ring and bundles of F-actin associated with the sperm cell nucleus disassembled (Figure 2D; Video 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2D and Video 2.

claim: F-actin assembles transient dynamic structures dedicated for fertilization.
source: Upon completion of karyogamy, the micropylar actin ring and bundles of F-actin associated with the sperm cell nucleus disassembled (Figure 2D; Video 2), suggesting that F-actin assembles transient dynamic structures dedicated for fertilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that F-actin structures disassemble after karyogamy.

claim: Constitutive expression of DN-ACTIN in the central cell prevented fertilization (Line 1, 30% defects).
source: The constitutive expression of DN-ACTIN in the central cell prevented fertilization [Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Line 1, 30% defects in DN-ACTIN (n = 120) compared to 0% defects in WT (n = 153)]
evidence: This is quantitative data from the DN-ACTIN experiment in central cells.

claim: Constitutive expression of DN-ACTIN in the central cell prevented endosperm development (Line 1, 25% defects).
source: The constitutive expression of DN-ACTIN in the central cell prevented fertilization [Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Line 1, 30% defects in DN-ACTIN (n = 120) compared to 0% defects in WT (n = 153)] and endosperm development [Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Line 1, 25% defects in DN-ACTIN (n = 412) compared to 0% defects in WT (n = 233)].
evidence: This is quantitative data from the DN-ACTIN experiment in central cells.

claim: Other independent transgenic lines expressing DN-ACTIN in the central cell showed similar rates of endosperm developmental defect (Line 2, 22% defects; Line 3, 21% defects).
source: Other independent transgenic lines expressing DN-ACTIN in the central cell also showed similar rates of endosperm developmental defect (Line 2, 22% defects [n = 300]; Line 3, 21% defects [n = 434]).
evidence: This is quantitative data from additional independent transgenic lines.

claim: Sperm cell fusion triggers central cell division.
source: Occasionally, a few nuclear divisions were observed in the endosperm (1–2%), resembling a phenotype described in ovules fertilized by cdka;1 sperm cells that are unable to undergo karyogamy (Aw et al., 2010), thus supporting further that sperm cell fusion triggers central cell division.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of nuclear divisions in the absence of karyogamy, similar to cdka;1 mutants, and supported by citation to Aw et al., 2010.

claim: F-actin plays an important role in fertilization of the central cell.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that F-actin also plays an important role in fertilization of the central cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the DN-ACTIN experiments showing fertilization and endosperm development defects.

claim: The FWA promoter is active soon after the central cell is determined.
source: Arabidopsis female gametes undergo a maturation phase once they become specified (Drews and Koltunow, 2011), and the FWA promoter is active soon after the central cell is determined.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the FWA promoter activity, with citation to Drews and Koltunow, 2011 for the maturation phase.

claim: A dexamethasone-inducible expression system was designed to activate DN-ACTIN after central cell maturation.
source: To overcome this problem, we designed a dexamethasone (DEX)-inducible expression system (Samalova et al., 2005) to activate DN-ACTIN after central cell maturation (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is described in the methods and illustrated in Figure 4A,B, with citation to Samalova et al., 2005.

claim: The P2A peptide causes ribosome skipping, generating two individual proteins from a single transgene.
source: During translation, the P2A sequence causes ribosome skipping, generating two individual proteins from a single transgene (El Amrani et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to El Amrani et al., 2004 and Kim et al., 2011.

claim: DN-ACTIN induced by DEX in the mature central cell disrupted F-actin organization and prevented sperm cell nucleus migration towards the female nucleus and karyogamy.
source: Consistent with the result from the constitutive expression of DN-ACTIN by the FWA promoter, DN-ACTIN induced by DEX in the mature central cell disrupted F-actin organization and prevented sperm cell nucleus migration towards the female nucleus and karyogamy (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figures 4C and 4E.

claim: DEX-induced DN-ACTIN prevented endosperm development.
source: Endosperm development was also prevented in DEX-treated plants (Figure 4D,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figures 4D and 4F.

claim: F-actin is essential for the migration of the sperm cell nucleus to the central cell nucleus.
source: These results confirmed that F-actin is essential for the migration of the sperm cell nucleus to the central cell nucleus.
evidence: This is concluded from the DEX-inducible DN-ACTIN experiments.

claim: Upon entry into the central cell, the sperm cell nucleus becomes surrounded by an increasing number of F-actin cables.
source: We observed that, upon entry into the central cell, the sperm cell nucleus becomes surrounded by an increasing number of F-actin cables (Figure 3A–D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3A-D.

claim: An aster-like structure of F-actin forms around the sperm cell nucleus after entry into the central cell.
source: followed by the formation of a dynamic aster-like structure around the sperm cell nucleus (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3E-H.

claim: The aster-like structure of F-actin was only observed around the sperm cell nucleus in the central cell after plasmogamy (100%, n = 48) and was never observed in unfertilized central cells (0%, n = 72).
source: This aster-like structure of F-actin was only observed around the sperm cell nucleus in the central cell after plasmogamy (100%, n = 48) and was never observed in unfertilized central cells (0%, n = 72).
evidence: This is quantitative data from observations of fertilized and unfertilized central cells.

claim: Time-lapse imaging showed the presence of aster-like F-actin structure only during sperm cell nucleus migration (100%, n = 5) and not in unfertilized ovules (0%, n = 14).
source: Consistently, the time-lapse imaging showed the presence of aster-like F-actin structure only during sperm cell nucleus migration [100% (n = 5); 0% in unfertilized ovule (n = 14)].
evidence: This is quantitative data from time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: The F-actin aster-like structure migrates together with the sperm cell nucleus towards the central cell nucleus.
source: The F-actin aster-like structure migrated together with the sperm cell nucleus towards the central cell nucleus (Video 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging data in Video 1.

claim: Specific actin regulators are involved in the formation and migration of the F-actin aster-like structure.
source: The F-actin aster-like structure migrated together with the sperm cell nucleus towards the central cell nucleus (Video 1), suggesting the involvement of specific actin regulators in this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of the dynamic aster-like structure.

claim: In plants, F-actin assembly is regulated by formins and ARP2/3 complex under the control of plant-specific Rho-GTPases (ROP).
source: In plants, F-actin assembly is regulated by formins and ARP2/3 complex under the control of plant-specific Rho-GTPases (ROP; Craddock et al., 2012; Henty-Ridilla et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant actin regulation, supported by citations to Craddock et al., 2012 and Henty-Ridilla et al., 2013.

claim: Transcriptional profiling suggested that ROP8 is specifically active in the central cell and the endosperm.
source: Transcriptional profiling (Borges et al., 2008; Le et al., 2010; Wuest et al., 2010; Belmonte et al., 2013) suggested that ROP8 is specifically active in the central cell and the endosperm (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on transcriptional profiling data from multiple studies, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The ROP8 promoter is specifically active in the central cell.
source: Indeed, we found that the ROP8 promoter is specifically active in the central cell (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 5B.

claim: Venus-ROP8 associates to the plasma membrane of the central cell.
source: and the fusion protein Venus-ROP8 associates to the plasma membrane of the central cell (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 5C.

claim: Ectopic expression of GFP-ROP8 showed its association to the plasma membrane in root epidermal cells.
source: Consistently, the ectopic expression of GFP-ROP8 also showed its association to the plasma membrane in root epidermal cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ROP8 sub-localization is controlled by general machinery common between the gametophytic central cell and somatic root epidermal cell.
source: indicating that ROP8 sub-localization is controlled by general machinery common between the gametophytic central cell and somatic root epidermal cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ROP8 localizes to the plasma membrane in both cell types.

claim: F-actin structures in both CA-ROP8 and DN-ROP8 appeared similar to wild-type.
source: Although F-actin structures in both CA-ROP8 and DN-ROP8 appeared similar to WT (Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: DN-ROP8 lines showed that the sperm cell chromatin in the central cell remained condensed and unfused with the central cell nucleus when the sperm cell chromatin had already fused with the egg cell nucleus.
source: only DN-ROP8 lines showed that the sperm cell chromatin in the central cell remained condensed and unfused with the central cell nucleus, when the sperm cell chromatin had already fused with the egg cell nucleus and appeared decondensed (Figure 5D; Line 1, 42% defects [n = 98], Line 2, 36% defects [n = 102]).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging and quantitative data in Figure 5D.

claim: DN-ROP8 Line 1 showed 42% fertilization defects in the central cell.
source: only DN-ROP8 lines showed that the sperm cell chromatin in the central cell remained condensed and unfused with the central cell nucleus, when the sperm cell chromatin had already fused with the egg cell nucleus and appeared decondensed (Figure 5D; Line 1, 42% defects [n = 98], Line 2, 36% defects [n = 102]).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the DN-ROP8 experiment.

claim: DN-ROP8 Line 2 showed 36% fertilization defects in the central cell.
source: only DN-ROP8 lines showed that the sperm cell chromatin in the central cell remained condensed and unfused with the central cell nucleus, when the sperm cell chromatin had already fused with the egg cell nucleus and appeared decondensed (Figure 5D; Line 1, 42% defects [n = 98], Line 2, 36% defects [n = 102]).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the DN-ROP8 experiment.

claim: The phenotype of DN-ROP8 was similar to the fertilization defect observed in central cells expressing DN-ACTIN.
source: This phenotype was similar to the fertilization defect observed in central cells expressing DN-ACTIN (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a comparison between the DN-ROP8 and DN-ACTIN phenotypes.

claim: A predominant F-actin movement from the cell periphery towards the nucleus (inward movement) occurs in the central cell.
source: We measured the dynamics of F-actin around the central cell nucleus, where the sperm cell nucleus migration occurs, and observed a predominant F-actin movement from the cell periphery towards the nucleus (Video 3), hereafter referred to as inward movement (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of F-actin dynamics shown in Figure 6A,B and Video 3.

claim: F-actin movement was extremely reduced in central cells expressing DN-ROP8.
source: By contrast, F-actin movement was extremely reduced in central cells expressing DN-ROP8 (Figure 6C–E; Videos 3; Video 4; Video 5; 45% and 30% defects in DN-ROP8 Line 1 [n = 11] and Line 2 [n = 10], respectively, compared to 0% defect in WT [n = 7] and CA-ROP8 Line 1 [n = 5] and Line 2 [n = 6]).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis and imaging data in Figure 6C-E and Videos 3-5.

claim: DN-ROP8 Line 1 showed 45% defects in F-actin movement.
source: By contrast, F-actin movement was extremely reduced in central cells expressing DN-ROP8 (Figure 6C–E; Videos 3; Video 4; Video 5; 45% and 30% defects in DN-ROP8 Line 1 [n = 11] and Line 2 [n = 10], respectively, compared to 0% defect in WT [n = 7] and CA-ROP8 Line 1 [n = 5] and Line 2 [n = 6]).
evidence: This is quantitative data from F-actin dynamics analysis.

claim: DN-ROP8 Line 2 showed 30% defects in F-actin movement.
source: By contrast, F-actin movement was extremely reduced in central cells expressing DN-ROP8 (Figure 6C–E; Videos 3; Video 4; Video 5; 45% and 30% defects in DN-ROP8 Line 1 [n = 11] and Line 2 [n = 10], respectively, compared to 0% defect in WT [n = 7] and CA-ROP8 Line 1 [n = 5] and Line 2 [n = 6]).
evidence: This is quantitative data from F-actin dynamics analysis.

claim: ROP8 controls novel constant inward dynamics of F-actin movement in the central cell.
source: Taken together, these results show that ROP8 controls novel constant inward dynamics of F-actin movement in the central cell
evidence: This is concluded from the F-actin dynamics analysis in WT and DN-ROP8 central cells.

claim: ROP8-dependent inward F-actin movement is required for the proper transport of the sperm cell nucleus to the central cell nucleus.
source: and that this ROP8-dependent inward F-actin movement is required for the proper transport of the sperm cell nucleus to the central cell nucleus.
evidence: This is concluded from the fertilization defects observed in DN-ROP8 lines.

claim: F-actin disassembly takes place around the central cell nucleus.
source: Although F-actin flows towards the central cell nucleus, we did not detect accumulation of F-actin around the nucleus (Video 3), suggesting that F-actin disassembly takes place around the central cell nucleus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that F-actin flows inward but does not accumulate around the nucleus.

claim: In plants, the motor protein myosin generates force to transport organelles along actin filaments within a cell.
source: In plants, the motor protein myosin generates force to transport organelles along actin filaments within a cell (Madison and Nebenfuhr, 2013), including the nuclear movement in somatic cells (Tamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about myosin function in plants, supported by citations to Madison and Nebenfuhr, 2013 and Tamura et al., 2013.

claim: Myosin is involved in nuclear movement in plant somatic cells.
source: In plants, the motor protein myosin generates force to transport organelles along actin filaments within a cell (Madison and Nebenfuhr, 2013), including the nuclear movement in somatic cells (Tamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tamura et al., 2013.

claim: In the presence of myosin inhibitors BDM or NEM, F-actin movement significantly reduced as observed in central cells expressing DN-ROP8.
source: In the presence of either myosin inhibitor, F-actin movement significantly reduced as observed in central cells expressingDN-ROP8 (Figure 6C–E; Videos 6; Video 7; 100% defect with BDM [n = 11] and NEM [n = 7], compared to 0% defect in mock treated ovules [n = 7 and 5, respectively]).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis and imaging data in Figure 6C-E and Videos 6-7.

claim: BDM treatment caused 100% defect in F-actin movement (n = 11).
source: In the presence of either myosin inhibitor, F-actin movement significantly reduced as observed in central cells expressingDN-ROP8 (Figure 6C–E; Videos 6; Video 7; 100% defect with BDM [n = 11] and NEM [n = 7], compared to 0% defect in mock treated ovules [n = 7 and 5, respectively]).
evidence: This is quantitative data from myosin inhibitor experiments.

claim: NEM treatment caused 100% defect in F-actin movement (n = 7).
source: In the presence of either myosin inhibitor, F-actin movement significantly reduced as observed in central cells expressingDN-ROP8 (Figure 6C–E; Videos 6; Video 7; 100% defect with BDM [n = 11] and NEM [n = 7], compared to 0% defect in mock treated ovules [n = 7 and 5, respectively]).
evidence: This is quantitative data from myosin inhibitor experiments.

claim: Myosin plays a role in the dynamics of F-actin in the central cell.
source: These results indicate that myosin plays a role in the dynamics of F-actin in the central cell and contributes to a net inward F-actin movement.
evidence: This is concluded from the myosin inhibitor experiments.

claim: Myosin contributes to a net inward F-actin movement in the central cell.
source: These results indicate that myosin plays a role in the dynamics of F-actin in the central cell and contributes to a net inward F-actin movement.
evidence: This is concluded from the myosin inhibitor experiments showing reduced inward F-actin movement.

claim: POR encodes a subunit of TUBULIN FOLDING COFACTOR C.
source: To investigate the requirement of microtubules in Arabidopsis fertilization, we used a null mutant allele of PORCINO (POR) that encodes a subunit of TUBULIN FOLDING COFACTOR C (Steinborn et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steinborn et al., 2002.

claim: Self-pollinated por/+ heterozygous plants produce about 25% defective embryos that do not assemble microtubule and abort.
source: Self-pollinated por/+ heterozygous plants produce about 25% defective embryos that do not assemble microtubule and abort, indicating that viable por gametes fuse to produce por/por homozygous seeds that are not viable (Steinborn et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steinborn et al., 2002.

claim: Viable por gametes fuse to produce por/por homozygous seeds that are not viable.
source: Self-pollinated por/+ heterozygous plants produce about 25% defective embryos that do not assemble microtubule and abort, indicating that viable por gametes fuse to produce por/por homozygous seeds that are not viable (Steinborn et al., 2002).
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic analysis and supported by citation to Steinborn et al., 2002.

claim: About half of the female gametes from por/+ mutants did not show microtubule structures.
source: In contrast to WT, about half of the female gametes from por/+ mutants did not show microtubule structures (Figure 7A,B,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging and quantitative data in Figure 7A,B,F.

claim: The proportion of por/+ female gametes without microtubule structures was consistent with the requirement of POR function for microtubule assembly.
source: This proportion was consistent with the requirement of POR function for microtubule assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the expected Mendelian ratio in por/+ heterozygotes.

claim: Wild-type and por mutant female gametes fertilized with either wild-type or por sperm cells showed successful karyogamy leading to the decondensation of chromatin from the sperm cell nucleus.
source: WT and por mutant female gametes fertilized with either WT or por sperm cells showed successful karyogamy leading to the decondensation of chromatin from the sperm cell nucleus (Figure 7C,D; 97% in WT [n = 102] and 96% in por/+ [n = 96]).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging and quantitative data in Figure 7C,D.

claim: 97% of wild-type ovules showed successful karyogamy (n = 102).
source: WT and por mutant female gametes fertilized with either WT or por sperm cells showed successful karyogamy leading to the decondensation of chromatin from the sperm cell nucleus (Figure 7C,D; 97% in WT [n = 102] and 96% in por/+ [n = 96]).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the por mutant analysis.

claim: 96% of por/+ ovules showed successful karyogamy (n = 96).
source: WT and por mutant female gametes fertilized with either WT or por sperm cells showed successful karyogamy leading to the decondensation of chromatin from the sperm cell nucleus (Figure 7C,D; 97% in WT [n = 102] and 96% in por/+ [n = 96]).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the por mutant analysis.

claim: Fertilization takes place despite defective microtubule assembly.
source: Taken together, these results show that fertilization takes place despite defective microtubule assembly and as a result, por/por embryo and endosperm development initiates.
evidence: This is concluded from the por mutant analysis showing successful karyogamy in the absence of microtubules.

claim: por/por embryo and endosperm development initiates despite defective microtubule assembly.
source: Taken together, these results show that fertilization takes place despite defective microtubule assembly and as a result, por/por embryo and endosperm development initiates.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding the other subunits (A, D and E) of TUBULIN FOLDING COFACTOR cause a seed abortion phenotype similar to that described in por.
source: Mutations in genes encoding the other subunits (A, D and E) of TUBULIN FOLDING COFACTOR cause a seed abortion phenotype similar to that described in por (Steinborn et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steinborn et al., 2002.

claim: Microtubules are not absolutely required for fertilization in Arabidopsis.
source: Mutations in genes encoding the other subunits (A, D and E) of TUBULIN FOLDING COFACTOR cause a seed abortion phenotype similar to that described in por (Steinborn et al., 2002), further demonstrating that microtubules are not absolutely required for fertilization in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is concluded from the analysis of multiple tubulin folding cofactor mutants.

claim: Microtubule organization was not affected in central cells expressing DN-ACTIN.

claim: In por central cells, the actin cytoskeleton retained its organization similar to wild-type.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton is the primary factor controlling sperm cell nuclear migration during fertilization in Arabidopsis in contrast to most animal species in which microtubules play a major role in pronuclear migration.
source: These observations support the idea that the actin cytoskeleton is the primary factor controlling sperm cell nuclear migration during fertilization in Arabidopsis in contrast to most animal species in which microtubules play a major role in pronuclear migration.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined observations of F-actin requirement and microtubule dispensability.

claim: Nuclear movement in both gamete and somatic cells has been extensively studied in animals.
source: Nuclear movement in both gamete and somatic cells has been extensively studied in animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Pronuclear migration in the fertilized egg is microtubule dependent in animals.
source: Pronuclear migration in the fertilized egg is microtubule dependent, but both actin filament and microtubules are indispensable for nuclear positioning in many somatic cells (Reinsch and Gonczy, 1998; Gundersen and Worman, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about animal cell biology, supported by citations to Reinsch and Gonczy, 1998 and Gundersen and Worman, 2013.

claim: Both actin filament and microtubules are indispensable for nuclear positioning in many animal somatic cells.
source: Pronuclear migration in the fertilized egg is microtubule dependent, but both actin filament and microtubules are indispensable for nuclear positioning in many somatic cells (Reinsch and Gonczy, 1998; Gundersen and Worman, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about animal cell biology, supported by citations to Reinsch and Gonczy, 1998 and Gundersen and Worman, 2013.

claim: Nuclear positioning during cell division and photo-relocation as well as tip growth of root hair and pollen tube has been investigated in plants.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Takagi et al., 2011 and Higa et al., 2014.

claim: Actin filaments play a critical role in nuclear positioning events in plant somatic cells.
source: and actin filaments play a critical role in these nuclear positioning events in plant somatic cells.

claim: Very little was known about gamete nuclear migration in plants.
source: By contrast, very little was known about gamete nuclear migration in plants.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: The centrosome loss in spermatogenous cells of land plants did not coincide with either the centrosome loss in somatic cells or the initiation of the actin-based organelle movement system in plants.

claim: Gamete nuclear migration in flowering plants might depend on a distinct mechanism from somatic cell nuclear positioning.

claim: The dynamic F-actin movement towards the central cell nucleus from the cell periphery constantly occurs prior to the sperm cell nucleus entry.
source: Here, we identified that the dynamic F-actin movement towards the central cell nucleus from the cell periphery constantly occurs prior to the sperm cell nucleus entry, and this F-actin movement is essential for sperm cell nucleus migration in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging and F-actin dynamics analysis.

claim: The dynamic F-actin movement towards the central cell nucleus is essential for sperm cell nucleus migration in Arabidopsis.
source: Here, we identified that the dynamic F-actin movement towards the central cell nucleus from the cell periphery constantly occurs prior to the sperm cell nucleus entry, and this F-actin movement is essential for sperm cell nucleus migration in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is concluded from the DN-ACTIN and DN-ROP8 experiments showing migration defects.

claim: The dynamic F-actin movement in the central cell is controlled by gamete-specific Rho-GTPase ROP8.
source: We also found that this dynamic F-actin movement in the central cell is controlled by gamete-specific Rho-GTPase ROP8 and is myosin dependent.
evidence: This is concluded from the DN-ROP8 experiments showing reduced F-actin dynamics.

claim: The dynamic F-actin movement in the central cell is myosin dependent.
source: We also found that this dynamic F-actin movement in the central cell is controlled by gamete-specific Rho-GTPase ROP8 and is myosin dependent.
evidence: This is concluded from the myosin inhibitor experiments showing reduced F-actin dynamics.

claim: Sperm cell nuclear migration in flowering plants is controlled by a novel actin-based mechanism that generates a constant F-actin inward movement towards the central cell nucleus.
source: Taken together, our results show that the sperm cell nuclear migration in flowering plants is controlled by a novel actin-based mechanism that generates a constant F-actin inward movement towards the central cell nucleus.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on all the experimental findings.

claim: The dynamic movement of F-actin towards the central nucleus, F-actin aster-like structure around the sperm cell nucleus during migration, and precise spatio-temporal disruption of F-actin after central cell maturation by the DEX system suggest direct involvement of F-actin for sperm cell nuclear migration.
source: The dynamic movement of F-actin towards the central nucleus, F-actin aster-like structure around the sperm cell nucleus during migration, and precise spatio-temporal disruption of F-actin after central cell maturation by the DEX system suggest direct involvement of F-actin for sperm cell nuclear migration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined experimental observations.

claim: It remains to be determined whether F-actin directly interacts with the sperm cell nucleus for migration.
source: However, it still remains to be determined whether F-actin directly interacts with the sperm cell nucleus for migration.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the current study.

claim: The central cell features a ring-shaped actin network at the micropylar end that surrounds the egg apparatus.
source: We also describe that F-actin is organized as unique structures in the central cell. In addition to the F-actin aster-like structure and the F-actin track that associate with the sperm cell nucleus migration, the central cell features a ring-shaped actin network at the micropylar end that surrounds the egg apparatus (the synergid cells and the egg cell).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2.

claim: The F-actin ring might maintain the position of the egg apparatus for fertilization.
source: The F-actin ring might maintain the position of the egg apparatus for fertilization or it might act as a clamp to maintain mechanical constraints that are required for efficient sperm cell delivery.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of the F-actin ring.

claim: The F-actin ring might act as a clamp to maintain mechanical constraints that are required for efficient sperm cell delivery.
source: The F-actin ring might maintain the position of the egg apparatus for fertilization or it might act as a clamp to maintain mechanical constraints that are required for efficient sperm cell delivery.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of the F-actin ring.

claim: All three organized F-actin structures become disassembled upon completion of karyogamy.
source: Upon completion of karyogamy, all three organized F-actin structures become disassembled, suggesting that these unique actin structures are specialized to achieve fertilization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2D and Video 2.

claim: The unique actin structures in the central cell are specialized to achieve fertilization.
source: Upon completion of karyogamy, all three organized F-actin structures become disassembled, suggesting that these unique actin structures are specialized to achieve fertilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these structures disassemble after karyogamy.

claim: Rho-GTPases are well-studied signaling factors controlling cytoskeleton dynamics.
source: Rho-GTPases are well-studied signaling factors controlling cytoskeleton dynamics (Yang, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citation to Yang, 2002.

claim: The constant inward movement of F-actin from the cell periphery to the nucleus occurs prior to fertilization in the wild-type central cell.

source: and this constant inward movement becomes significantly reduced in DN-ROP8, but not in CA-ROP8 transgenic lines.

claim: ROP8 might be constantly active in the entire central cell plasma membrane, generating a constitutive dynamic inward movement of F-actin.
source: These results suggest that ROP8 might be constantly active in the entire central cell plasma membrane, generating a constitutive dynamic inward movement of F-actin.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The putative constant active mode of ROP8 in the central cell could explain why DN-ROP8, but not CA-ROP8 transgenic lines affected F-actin dynamics significantly.
source: This could explain why DN-ROP8, but not CA-ROP8 transgenic lines affected F-actin dynamics significantly (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference to explain the differential effects of DN-ROP8 and CA-ROP8.

claim: The activation/inactivation of ROPs is generally controlled spatially at the plasma membrane, generating subdomains within a cell for downstream events.
source: In general, the activation/inactivation of ROPs is controlled spatially at the plasma membrane, generating subdomains within a cell for downstream events such as secondary cell wall formation (Oda and Fukuda, 2012) and pavement cell indentation (Xu et al., 2010).

evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: F-actin function is important for sperm cell nuclear migration in the Arabidopsis egg cell.

evidence: This is based on established knowledge from somatic cells, supported by citation to Tamura et al., 2013.
